idiom_name: hand-written wrapper function over the audited operation + syslog(3) sink
implementation_notes: C has no interception machinery, so the interceptor is a wrapper function that records the event and then calls the audited operation through the pointer it was installed in place of: the classic Interceptor/InvocationContext structure is replaced by a function-pointer (or vtable-slot) indirection, with the saved real function as the delegation target and a context struct carrying the actor and the operation name. Use syslog(3) (with openlog(), a LOG_AUTH/LOG_AUTHPRIV facility and a fixed format string) or a dedicated append-only file/journald API as the sink. Because there is no reflection, every audited operation needs its own wrapper or a table-driven shim with a per-operation descriptor, and the manual form remains the only option when auditing must be retrofitted without touching the implementation.
pitfalls: Interception depends on every caller using the installed pointer: a direct call to the real symbol (or a cached copy of it) bypasses the wrapper without any diagnostic.
Writing to syslog or a file from inside a signal handler or a held lock can deadlock or lose records; hand events to a queue and let one thread own the sink.
Never pass caller-controlled data as the format string of syslog(3) (use syslog(pri, "%s", s)); format-string bugs turn the audit sink into an injection surface.
